title: Nuun vs LMNT: Which Electrolyte Mix Is Better for You?
excerpt: Nuun vs LMNT compared: sodium, sugar, price, taste, and which one makes sense for hangovers, workouts, keto, and everyday hydration.
metaDescription: Nuun vs LMNT: sodium, sugar, price, and taste compared, plus which one fits hangovers, workouts, keto, and everyday hydration.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Nuun and LMNT are both low-sugar electrolyte mixes, but they sit at opposite ends of the salt scale. A Nuun Sport tablet has roughly 300 mg of sodium and makes a light, fizzy drink you can sip all day. An LMNT stick has roughly 1,000 mg of sodium, more than three times as much, and is built for heavy sweaters, long training sessions, and people eating low-carb or fasting. Neither has enough sugar to work like a classic oral rehydration drink. For most social drinkers rehydrating after a night out, Nuun is the gentler, cheaper everyday pick, and LMNT makes more sense only if you sweated a lot, threw up, or already know you do well on extra salt. Neither one is a hangover cure, and LMNT in particular is a poor daily habit for anyone with high blood pressure, kidney disease, or heart problems unless a doctor says otherwise.

**The quick picks:**

- **Light rehydration, desk sipping, short workouts:** Nuun Sport, one tablet in 16 ounces of water.
- **Long, hot, sweaty sessions or salty sweaters:** LMNT, one stick in 16 to 32 ounces.
- **Keto, low-carb, or fasting:** LMNT, usually diluted in a full 32 ounces.
- **The morning after drinking:** either can help with the fluid part. Nuun is easier on a queasy stomach; LMNT should go in a full quart of water, not a small glass.
- **Before bed after drinking:** a non-caffeinated Nuun, a well-diluted LMNT, or just plain water. Not a caffeinated tablet.
- **High blood pressure, kidney or heart disease, or told to limit salt:** ask your doctor first. If you get the OK, Nuun is the lower-sodium starting point.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article compares general label information and research. It is not a substitute for a doctor who knows your health history. **Talk to a doctor before using electrolyte mixes regularly if** you have high blood pressure, kidney disease, heart failure, or diabetes, you've been told to limit salt, fluids, or potassium, you're pregnant, or you take medicines that affect sodium or potassium (some blood pressure pills, water pills, and potassium-sparing drugs, for example). **Get medical help right away if** someone who has been drinking is confused, very hard to wake, breathing slowly or irregularly, has cold, clammy, or blue-tinged skin, has a seizure, or can't stop vomiting. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, not a hangover. In the US, call 911. Product formulas change, so check the current package for exact numbers.

## Nuun vs LMNT at a Glance

These are approximate per-serving figures for each brand's flagship product, based on the published labels at the time of writing. Both companies sell several sub-lines with different recipes, so always read the box you're holding.

| | Nuun Sport (tablet) | LMNT (standard stick) |
|---|---|---|
| Format | Effervescent tablet you drop in water | Powder stick you stir or shake in |
| Sodium | ~300 mg | ~1,000 mg |
| Potassium | ~150 mg | ~200 mg |
| Magnesium | ~25 mg | ~60 mg |
| Calcium | A small amount | None to speak of |
| Sugar | ~1 g | 0 g |
| Calories | ~15 | ~10 or less |
| Sweetener | Mostly stevia | Stevia (the "Raw" version is unsweetened) |
| Caffeine | None in plain Sport; some Nuun flavors and lines contain caffeine | None in the standard sticks |
| Added vitamins | Few in Sport; other Nuun lines add vitamins | None to speak of |
| Suggested water | 16 fl oz | 16 to 32 fl oz |
| Typical price per serving | Often under $1 | Roughly $1.50, less with bulk or subscription |
| Where to buy | Widely: grocery stores, pharmacies, sporting goods, online | Mostly direct from the brand and online, with growing retail presence |

The headline difference: **LMNT is a salt delivery system. Nuun is a lightly salted, lightly flavored drink.** Almost every "which is better" question comes down to how much sodium you actually need that day.

## Who Makes Them, and What Each Was Designed For

The two brands came from different worlds, and their formulas show it.

**Nuun** started as a tablet for endurance athletes who wanted to replace the salt they lost in sweat without drinking a sugary sports drink. The fizzy tablet format came from that goal: it's small, it dissolves on its own, and it makes a drink that tastes only mildly salty. Nuun Sport is still the core product. Over the years the company added other lines with different jobs, including versions with added vitamins, versions with caffeine, an endurance version with more carbohydrate, and a calming evening-style formula. Nuun is now owned by Nestlé Health Science.

**LMNT** came out of the low-carb and paleo community. It was co-founded by Robb Wolf, a writer well known in that world, and the brand's message is that many active people, and especially people eating very few carbohydrates, are under-salted. When you cut carbs sharply, your kidneys shed more sodium and water for a while, which is a large part of what people call the "keto flu." A full gram of sodium per stick is a deliberate answer to that problem, not a typo.

So Nuun was built to be pleasant enough to sip all day. LMNT was built to deliver a large, specific dose of salt with no sugar at all.

## The Biggest Difference: How Salty the Drink Is

The fairest way to compare electrolyte drinks is by concentration, meaning how salty the finished drink is, not just what's printed on the package. You choose how much water to use, and that changes everything.

- **Nuun Sport in 16 oz:** about 300 mg of sodium in roughly half a liter. That works out to about 28 millimoles of sodium per liter (millimoles are just a way of counting how many sodium particles are in the drink).
- **LMNT in 16 oz:** about 1,000 mg in half a liter, or roughly 90 millimoles per liter. That's saltier than the World Health Organization's reduced-osmolarity oral rehydration solution, which contains 75 millimoles per liter, and it tastes like it.
- **LMNT in 32 oz:** the same 1,000 mg spread across about a liter, or roughly 45 millimoles per liter.

Put plainly, **one LMNT stick in a quart of water is still more than one and a half times as salty as a Nuun tablet in a pint.** And because you're drinking a full quart, you take in more than three times the total sodium.

Many people find LMNT unpleasantly salty at 16 ounces. If that's you, the fix is more water, not a different product. Going the other way, Nuun can taste a bit thin if you're used to sports drinks, but adding a second tablet doubles the sodium, so think about why you want it stronger before you do that.

### How much sodium is too much?

US dietary guidelines suggest most adults keep sodium under about 2,300 mg a day, and the American Heart Association points to 1,500 mg as an ideal target for many adults, especially those with high blood pressure. Most people already eat more than that from food alone.

- **One Nuun tablet** uses about 13 percent of the 2,300 mg figure. Two or three across a day is a manageable amount for most healthy people.
- **One LMNT stick** uses nearly half of it. Two sticks plus a normal day of food will put most people well over the limit.

That doesn't make LMNT dangerous for a healthy, active person who's losing a lot of salt in sweat, because sweat can carry away a lot of sodium. It does mean LMNT isn't a casual "sip it all day at my desk" drink for most people. It's a tool for days when you've actually lost salt. Nuun is closer to something you can drink on an ordinary day without doing much math.

## The Second Difference: Neither One Has Much Sugar

This is where Nuun and LMNT are more alike than different, and it's worth understanding because it affects how well either one rehydrates you.

Your small intestine has a transporter that pulls sodium and glucose into your body together, and water follows them. That's the principle behind oral rehydration solutions, the simple salt-and-sugar drinks used to treat dehydration from diarrhea. It's why brands such as Liquid I.V. and Pedialyte deliberately include sugar.

- **Nuun Sport** has about a gram of sugar, which is a token amount. It's mainly there for taste.
- **LMNT** has none at all.

So neither product is designed as an oral rehydration drink. They rely on sodium and the water you mix them with. For someone who is mildly short on fluid and eating normally, that's fine: food supplies the glucose, and the water and salt do the rest. For someone who is genuinely dehydrated, can't keep food down, or has had vomiting or diarrhea, a drink built on the ORS formula is the better tool. We compare those in our [Liquid I.V. vs Pedialyte guide](/never-hungover/liquid-iv-vs-pedialyte-for-hangover).

There's an easy workaround if you like the taste of Nuun or LMNT but want a little glucose: drink it alongside some toast, a banana, or a bowl of cereal. That pairs the salt with carbohydrate in your gut without changing the drink.

## Potassium and Magnesium: Smaller Differences Than They Look

Both brands add potassium and magnesium, and LMNT has a bit more of each per serving. In practice, neither delivers a large share of what you need in a day.

- **Potassium:** adults need several thousand milligrams a day from food. Nuun's ~150 mg and LMNT's ~200 mg are both small next to a single banana or potato. Potassium matters for muscle and nerve function, and alcohol does increase how much you lose in urine, but food is the main way to restore it.
- **Magnesium:** LMNT's ~60 mg is more meaningful than Nuun's ~25 mg, but both are well below a daily target of a few hundred milligrams. Regular heavy drinking is linked to low magnesium over time, which is a diet and drinking-pattern issue rather than something a drink mix fixes.

If you're choosing between the two, potassium and magnesium shouldn't be the deciding factor. Sodium and price will matter far more.

## Nuun vs LMNT for a Hangover

This is the question most of our readers are actually asking, so here's the plain version.

### What alcohol does to your fluids

Alcohol makes you pee more than you drink. It lowers a hormone called vasopressin (also called antidiuretic hormone), which normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water. With less of that signal, your kidneys let more water go, along with some sodium and potassium. Add sweating in a warm bar, dancing, or vomiting, and you lose more. Our explainer on [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) goes into the details.

### What an electrolyte drink can and can't do

Replacing fluid can help with the dry mouth, thirst, and some of the headache and dizziness that come from being short on fluid. That's real, and it's why people feel better after a big glass of something salty.

But dehydration is only one part of a hangover. Researchers who study hangovers have found that dehydration and hangover severity are related, yet dehydration on its own doesn't explain how bad people feel. Poor sleep, inflammation, low blood sugar, and the by-products your body makes while breaking down alcohol all play a part. There is no good evidence that any electrolyte drink, Nuun and LMNT included, prevents or cures a hangover. They help with one slice of the problem.

### Which one to reach for

- **You feel thirsty and a bit off, but your stomach is fine:** either works. Nuun is the lighter, cheaper option. LMNT in a full 32 ounces is fine too.
- **You sweated a lot or threw up once or twice:** LMNT has the edge here because you've actually lost salt. Mix it in a full 32 ounces and sip it over an hour or so rather than gulping it.
- **You feel nauseous:** start with small sips. Nuun's lighter, fizzy taste is easier for many people. A very salty drink on a queasy stomach can make nausea worse.
- **You can't keep fluids down, or you've had repeated vomiting or diarrhea:** an oral rehydration solution is a better fit than either product, and if you still can't keep anything down after several hours, see a doctor.

Our full guide on [LMNT for a hangover](/never-hungover/lmnt-for-hangover) goes deeper on using LMNT specifically, and our step-by-step guide on [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking) covers the order of operations: water first, food soon, electrolytes as a helper.

### Skip the caffeinated Nuun around drinking

Some Nuun flavors and lines contain caffeine, often roughly the amount in a small cup of coffee. That's worth avoiding in two situations: while you're drinking, because caffeine can make you feel less drunk than you are without lowering your blood alcohol, and late at night after drinking, because it can make the already-poor sleep after alcohol worse. Check the package, since the caffeinated tubes can look very similar to the plain ones. Standard LMNT sticks are caffeine-free.

## Nuun vs LMNT Before Drinking

Some people take electrolytes before going out, hoping to start the night well hydrated. That's reasonable as long as you keep expectations modest.

Starting the evening properly hydrated is a sensible habit, but it doesn't change how fast you absorb alcohol or how your body breaks it down. A Nuun tablet in a glass of water before you go out is a fine, low-salt way to do that. A full LMNT stick before a night of salty bar food and drinks adds a lot of sodium on top of what you'll already eat, so if you use LMNT, a half stick in a big glass of water is plenty.

The habits that make the biggest difference are still the simple ones: eat a real meal, alternate alcoholic drinks with water, and drink less. Our guide on [whether to take electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) looks at timing in more detail, and [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

## Nuun vs LMNT for Keto, Low-Carb, and Fasting

This is LMNT's home turf. When you sharply cut carbohydrates, your body lowers insulin, and lower insulin tells your kidneys to release more sodium and water. That's why many people feel tired, headachy, and lightheaded in the first week or two of a low-carb diet. Extra sodium often eases those symptoms, and LMNT was designed with exactly that in mind.

- **LMNT** fits strict keto and fasting well: zero sugar, zero meaningful calories, and enough sodium to make a difference.
- **Nuun Sport** has about a gram of sugar and around 15 calories per tablet. That's very little, and most people on keto would have no trouble fitting it in. Whether it "breaks a fast" depends on how strict your rules are. It also has much less sodium, so you'd need more tablets to get the same effect, which defeats the purpose.

If you're on keto and also drink alcohol, it's worth knowing that many people report lower alcohol tolerance on a low-carb diet. Pace yourself.

## Nuun vs LMNT for Workouts and Endurance

For a typical 30 to 60 minute gym session, most people don't need either one. Water is enough. Electrolytes start to matter more when sessions run long, the weather is hot, or you're a salty sweater (if your workout clothes dry with white salt marks, that's probably you).

- **Short to moderate sessions:** Nuun Sport is a nice upgrade over plain water if you like the taste. It adds a little salt without much else.
- **Long, hot sessions, or heavy, salty sweat:** LMNT's higher sodium makes more sense. Endurance athletes sometimes use it diluted in a large bottle across a long effort.
- **Long endurance efforts where you need fuel:** neither standard product provides meaningful carbohydrate. Nuun's endurance line adds more, and many athletes pair either product with gels, chews, or food.

## Price, Format, and Taste

These practical details often decide the question once you've figured out how much salt you need.

**Price.** Nuun is usually the cheaper option per serving, often under a dollar a tablet in multi-tube packs. LMNT tends to run about $1.50 a stick, less with bulk boxes or subscriptions. If you plan to drink electrolytes most days, that gap adds up.

**Format.** Nuun's tablets come in a slim tube that fits in a bag or jacket pocket and dissolve on their own in a couple of minutes, but you need to wait for the fizz to settle before capping a bottle. LMNT's sticks pour in instantly and are easy to split in half, which is handy if you find a full stick too salty. LMNT also sells a canned sparkling version.

**Taste.** Nuun tastes light and lightly fizzy, a bit like flavored sparkling water with a hint of salt. LMNT tastes clearly salty, especially in less water, and some flavors are fairly intense. People who like LMNT often say the saltiness feels "right" after a sweaty session. People who don't like it usually say it tastes like seawater. A cheap way to test is to buy a small sample pack of each before committing to a box.

**Where to buy.** Nuun is easy to find in grocery stores, pharmacies, and sporting goods stores. LMNT is sold mostly online and direct from the brand, with more retail availability than it used to have.

## Which Is Healthier?

Neither is unhealthy for a typical adult using them sensibly, and neither is necessary for most people on most days. Food and water cover everyday needs.

The real health question is sodium. If your doctor has told you to watch your salt, or you have high blood pressure, kidney disease, or heart failure, LMNT's full gram of sodium per stick is a lot to add to your day, and Nuun's 300 mg still counts. Talk to your doctor before using either one regularly.

A couple of other points worth knowing:

- **Sweeteners.** Both use stevia in most flavors. Some people find stevia leaves an aftertaste or upsets their stomach. LMNT's unsweetened "Raw" option avoids it.
- **Caffeine.** Some Nuun products contain caffeine; standard LMNT does not. If you're sensitive to caffeine or drinking electrolytes in the evening, read the label.
- **Kidney and medication concerns.** Potassium amounts in both are modest, but people on potassium-sparing medicines or with kidney disease should still check with their doctor.

## Can You Use Both?

Yes. Plenty of people keep both around: Nuun for ordinary days and casual sipping, LMNT for long, sweaty sessions or a rough morning after a lot of sweating. There's nothing wrong with mixing brands across a week. Just keep a rough count of your total sodium, and don't drink a Nuun and an LMNT back to back "to double up." If you need that much salt, one LMNT in plenty of water is the simpler choice.

If you'd rather not buy either, a basic homemade mix of water, a pinch of salt, and a splash of juice does a similar job for a fraction of the price. Our [homemade electrolyte drink guide](/never-hungover/homemade-electrolyte-drink) has simple recipes.

## How Nuun and LMNT Compare to Other Options

If you're shopping around, here's how these two fit into the wider field:

- **Against Liquid I.V.:** Liquid I.V. sits between them on sodium (about 500 mg) and adds about 11 grams of sugar to work more like an oral rehydration drink. See our [Nuun vs Liquid I.V.](/never-hungover/nuun-vs-liquid-iv) and [LMNT vs Liquid I.V.](/never-hungover/lmnt-vs-liquid-iv) comparisons.
- **Against other high-sodium mixes:** if you like LMNT's approach but want to compare price and sodium per serving, see our [Saltt vs LMNT](/never-hungover/saltt-vs-lmnt) breakdown.
- **For a broad comparison:** our guide to [electrolyte drinks for a hangover](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared) lines up the major brands side by side, and [electrolytes and alcohol](/never-hungover/electrolytes-and-alcohol) explains which electrolytes alcohol actually affects.

## When to See a Doctor

Most hangovers are miserable but harmless and clear up within a day. An electrolyte drink is fine for that. But some symptoms are not a normal hangover, and no drink mix is the right response.

**Get help right away (call 911 in the US) if someone who has been drinking:**

- Is confused, very hard to wake, or can't be woken
- Is breathing slowly or irregularly
- Has cold, clammy, pale, or blue-tinged skin
- Has a seizure
- Is vomiting repeatedly, especially while very drowsy

**See a doctor soon if you:**

- Can't keep fluids down for several hours, or are barely urinating
- Feel dizzy or faint when you stand up, even after drinking fluids
- Have a racing or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle
- See blood in your vomit or stool, or have severe stomach pain
- Notice your hangovers are getting worse, or you get shaky, sweaty, or anxious when you haven't had a drink. That can be a sign your body has started depending on alcohol, and it's worth a straightforward conversation with a doctor.

## A Note on DHM

Electrolyte drinks deal with fluid loss after the fact. Some people also look at supplements that target how the body handles alcohol itself. The most studied of these is **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a plant compound researched for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the evidence comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven, and there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers on its own. It also doesn't replace water, food, or drinking less.

If you want to try it alongside sensible hydration, popular picks include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## The Bottom Line

- **Nuun** is a light, low-sugar, lower-sodium tablet (about 300 mg). It's the better everyday choice, cheaper per serving, easier on a queasy stomach, and the safer starting point if you're watching your salt.
- **LMNT** is a high-sodium, zero-sugar stick (about 1,000 mg). It's the better choice for heavy sweating, long hot sessions, keto, and fasting, and it should usually go in a full 32 ounces of water.
- **Neither** has enough sugar to act as a true oral rehydration drink, so pair them with food, or use an ORS-style product if you're genuinely dehydrated.
- **For a hangover,** either can help with the fluid part, and neither is a cure. Skip caffeinated Nuun flavors around drinking.
- **If you have high blood pressure, kidney disease, or heart failure,** talk to your doctor before using either one regularly.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is Nuun or LMNT better?**

It depends on how much salt you need. Nuun Sport has about 300 mg of sodium per tablet and suits everyday sipping, short workouts, and light rehydration. LMNT has about 1,000 mg per stick and suits heavy sweating, long hot sessions, keto, and fasting. For most people on an ordinary day, Nuun is the more sensible choice. LMNT is a tool for days when you've genuinely lost a lot of salt.

**Is Nuun or LMNT better for a hangover?**

Either can help with the dehydration part of a hangover, and neither is a cure. Nuun is gentler and easier on a queasy stomach. LMNT makes more sense if you sweated heavily or vomited, and it should be mixed into a full 32 ounces of water and sipped slowly. If you can't keep fluids down, an oral rehydration solution is a better fit than either, and you should see a doctor if that lasts several hours.

**How much more sodium does LMNT have than Nuun?**

About three times as much per serving. A standard LMNT stick has roughly 1,000 mg of sodium, while a Nuun Sport tablet has roughly 300 mg. Even when LMNT is diluted in 32 ounces of water and Nuun in 16 ounces, the LMNT drink is still more than one and a half times as salty, and you take in more than three times the total sodium.

**Which is better for keto or fasting, Nuun or LMNT?**

LMNT is generally the better fit. It has zero sugar and a large dose of sodium, which is what many people need when cutting carbs causes their kidneys to release more salt and water. Nuun Sport has about a gram of sugar and much less sodium, so you'd need several tablets to match one LMNT stick.

**Can I drink Nuun or LMNT every day?**

Most healthy adults can use one Nuun tablet a day without trouble. One LMNT stick uses up nearly half of the commonly recommended 2,300 mg daily sodium limit, so it's best kept for days when you're sweating a lot. If you have high blood pressure, kidney disease, or heart failure, or you've been told to limit salt, talk to your doctor before using either one regularly.

**Does Nuun have caffeine?**

Plain Nuun Sport doesn't, but some Nuun flavors and product lines do. Check the label, especially around drinking. Caffeine can make you feel less drunk than you are while drinking and can worsen sleep after a night out. Standard LMNT sticks are caffeine-free.

**Why does LMNT taste so salty?**

Because it's very salty. One stick in 16 ounces of water is saltier than the World Health Organization's oral rehydration formula. If it tastes too strong, mix it into 32 ounces of water, or use half a stick. That keeps the drink closer to the saltiness of other electrolyte mixes.

**Do Nuun or LMNT prevent hangovers?**

There is no good evidence that any electrolyte drink prevents or cures a hangover. Replacing fluid and salt can ease thirst, dry mouth, and some dizziness and headache, but hangovers also involve poor sleep, inflammation, and the by-products of breaking down alcohol. Eating, alternating drinks with water, and drinking less make a bigger difference.
